idiom_name: one coarse-grained owner for the cluster, persisted by a single unit of work
implementation_notes: Give the cluster exactly one coarse-grained object that owns the dependents and is the only entry point; let each dependent carry its own mapping knowledge instead of leaking it into clients. Load the graph through the root, mutate dependents only through root-level operations, and flush everything inside one transaction or unit of work, with the add/remove lifecycle of dependents expressed in the relationship so that removal deletes the orphan. Behind the relationship, declare the foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE (or an equivalent) so a partially persisted graph cannot survive a crash, and hand clients a coarse-grained transfer object rather than the live cluster.
code_sketch:
root = new CompositeEntity(id)
root.load()                       # dependents materialised as one unit
root.removeDependent(x)           # lifecycle owned by the root
unit_of_work.begin()
mapper.save(root)                 # root + dependents, one transaction
unit_of_work.commit()             # nothing partial survives
# clients: coarse_grained = root.toTransferObject()
pitfalls: Splitting the save across several transactions: the pattern's guarantee is the single unit of work, not the object shape.
Exposing the dependents (getters returning live children) lets callers save them individually and recreate the desynchronised graph the composite was meant to prevent.
Forgetting the dependent-removal rule (orphanRemoval / delete-orphan / cascade delete): rows stay in the store while the domain object believes they are gone.

Optimistic concurrency explosion: applying @Version or rowversion to the root causes conflicts when concurrent transactions modify different, unrelated dependents — the whole cluster is treated as one conflict unit.
N+1 in reverse: eager-loading the composite in one query cascades the join across all dependents, materialising the entire graph when only one dependent is needed.

Broken invariant at the cluster boundary: allowing callers to mutate dependent fields without going through the root's operation means consistency rules enforced only at the root are silently bypassed.
Cascade wildcard abuse: cascade=ALL persists any object that happens to be attached to the relationship at flush time, including objects the caller never intended to save.
Serialized LOB bloat: serialising a large or unbounded dependent graph into a single BLOB column defeats the purpose of the composite and creates garbage-collection and indexing problems.
Domain event handler outside the transaction boundary: firing events from within a dependent's setter rather than from the root's post-commit hook means subscribers see stale or rolled-back state.
Test fixture graph sharing: reusing the same in-memory composite instance across multiple test cases without deep-cloning causes non-deterministic test ordering and cross-test state leakage.

Aggregate divorce: the domain model declares one aggregate boundary but the persistence layer (or a developer bypass) splits the graph across multiple Unit-of-Work commits, violating the transactional invariant.

Wrong move: fold entities into the composite just because they are related; failure: a god aggregate with unbounded collections causes lock contention, long transactions and write amplification on every unrelated edit; instead: shrink the boundary to the invariant that must hold in one transaction and reference other clusters by id with eventual consistency.

Wrong move: update two composites inside one SaveChanges/Unit-of-Work commit; failure: the commit boundary silently spans clusters, so a rolled-back second aggregate reverts the first one's accepted invariants; instead: commit one composite per transaction and coordinate the rest with domain events.

Wrong move: navigate dependent collections solely through eagerly loaded navigation properties (Customer -> Orders -> OrderLines chains); failure: loading one root materialises an ever-growing graph and the composite degenerates into distributed-chatty object fetches; instead: keep references to other composites as ids and load them through their own root.
